title: Grand Theft Auto VI Is Really Weird
text:
J ason Duval lives in a shack on the Leonida Keys, in the simulated Florida where Grand Theft Auto VI is set. I began playing the game after its release at midnight, and I have already tried and failed to outrun the police, roamed the hallways of a prison, driven a speedboat to collect cocaine dropped by a seaplane pilot who was skimming from a more upmarket criminal, and flown the seaplane to escape an RV park full of wild-animal-and-narcotics traffickers.

 If you know anything at all about the game, which almost 5,000 people worked on for more than a decade at a reported cost of more than $1 billion, it is that Leonida is enormous. Early reviewers are bragging on social media about spending more than 100 hours in the world of the game, while only scratching the surface of what is possible. The prospect seems overwhelming because I already have a life that requires labor and demands diversion, and I am worried about how to fit GTA VI ’s simulated work and recreation into my supposedly real life.

 Theorists of video games (a real thing that I could be accused of being) have a name for this phenomenon: playbor , a portmanteau of play and labor . Many jobs feel fake now anyway—“email jobs,” they were scornfully called even before AI could be mustered to carry out their pointlessness—and games feel like jobs, with a seemingly endless list of menial tasks for their players.

 [ Read: The least productive day of the year ] 

 An hour or so in, though, the game offers a breather to look around and get your bearings. I decide to stay in Jason’s house instead of venturing out into even a tiny corner of Leonida. There is so much to do here that I find myself wondering how many hours I might spend indoors, inside the pretend home of a fake man. After all, I pass most of my own life as a real man inside my real home, working and puttering, instead of exploring the city or countryside that contain me.

 J ason has a pet snake, and walking by its glass habitat triggers a text overlay indicating that I can interact with it. I press a button to feed the snake, and Jason reaches into a blue plastic container, carefully retrieves a mouse, and drops it into the cage. I can see another mouse or two in there, of varied shades. I already feel as though I need to resupply the snake food. I find myself wondering where one goes for snake mice, and what that shop might be called in Grand Theft Auto .

 “Thoughtful actions will increase your focus bar,” the game tells me after I feed the animal. Feeding a snake is thoughtful, apparently. A purple icon animates and a corresponding purple bar fills slightly to communicate the effect of the act. Jason’s stamina and strength are also measured in health-bar form. Some games allocate a bar for hunger or even bladder level.

 This kind of thing used to seem ridiculous, a perverse way to understand human behavior for the nerds who design and play video games. But when I look at my real smartwatch on my actual wrist, I realize the world has caught up. It translates my movement into a number on a red bar that supposedly represents my activity. I don’t believe that the numbers—383 calories so far today—are real, but I orient my activities around them every day. Better do a quick Peloton to close my rings; time for another walk to get my steps in. I don’t think about it much anymore, but I have become a video-game avatar of myself.

 I n the shack, morning light pours across a desk from a window whose blinds are raised halfway. On the desk are a radio, a few books, and a conch shell. You know that a video-game object is relevant when it receives an overlay with a text description and an icon of the controller button used to interact with it. In this case, the radio’s channels can be changed with a button on my PlayStation 5 controller, and the book can be examined with a different button. I cannot interact with the conch.

 After flipping to a station called Afrobank FM, I examine the book. It’s called Orca: A Whole Different Animal . The book isn’t about killer whales. It’s a send-up of the Navy SEALs and the kind of inspirational title that a former officer might write as CEO of a private mercenary firm or in anticipation of running for a U.S. Senate seat. I can open the book, which contains actual text on simulated pages.

 I’ve read that Rockstar Games, the creator of GTA , did not use generative AI during the production of the game, and instead employs a large team of people who create all of the media inside it—including Orca , presumably. I wonder whether libraries or bookstores exist in the game, which I might then treat as a laborious literary experience rather than a criminal-underworld fantasy. But flipping through Orca reveals that the game surfaces only a few pages. The book is not real, in the sense that a book contains writing sufficient to justify a book. It is, instead, an icon of a book, like the conch is an icon for decor. I somewhat wish that Rockstar had used AI to generate books instead. I assume—I haven’t looked yet—that someone has, by now, generated a real, fake version of Orca: A Whole Different Animal and put it up for sale on Amazon.

 J ason’s eyes suggest an earnestness that makes me want to like him. The hairs at the top of the mustache stick out and up slightly, in a casual manner that suggests affability more than unkemptness. It seems remarkable to be able to interpret a character in this way, and I find myself suspicious of the matter. Not too long ago, an “uncanny valley” effect made computer characters seem unreal—they were immensely real but just shy of credible, and that gap made them slightly creepy. The gap appears to have been closed.

 Now, instead, I wonder whether I really like Jason or am being tricked into liking him by how well the game has established his plight. Earlier, he hooked up with Lucia Caminos, the game’s other protagonist, whom I had controlled as she committed a robbery that got her arrested. I’ve watched Jason tolerate a prolix conspiracy theorist named Cal and rescue a hot-mess smuggler named Donnie. His ex-military credentials have been established, and Jason’s all-American appearance suggests a good guy in a bad spot. The writing and characterization are good in the way a television show is these days—which is to say, too good, too clean. The paradox of fiction has become the new hurdle. I find myself worrying that my years of vocal skepticism about video-game storytelling are at risk of coming undone.

 W hen uncanniness persists, it offers me comfort. In the kitchen, I can make Jason pour a coffee and drink it. Doing so raises his focus and his stamina, as coffee is known to do. He drinks it so quickly that I worry about scalding him, but that is tempered by the realization that he didn’t really drink it—no liquid moves between the mug’s lip and Jason’s mouth, as if the mug had been a prop in a black-box theater production or a stop-motion animation. The simplest background acts of other narrative media, such as films or novels, require enormous amounts of engineering to accomplish in software. In a book, you can say, “Jason poured and drank a cup of coffee.” In a movie, you can point the camera at an actor doing so, and the act along with the liquid’s heat shimmer would be captured through the lens. But nothing is free in games.

 Jason continues holding the mug as I walk around his place. It dangles from his right hand like a cigarette. When he opens the fridge at the behest of a button press, he does so with his nonpreferred hand, so he can continue clinging to the mug. The game interprets the mug in the same way it would a pistol—an object is probably a weapon, one that you’d want to put down only deliberately.

 If I let go of the controller, Jason enters what game developers call an idle state. It would seem weird if a game simply stopped when the player isn’t doing something, so the software makes the characters bob and sway in a manner that seems realistic until it goes on too long. Jason’s body moves to the beat of the music on Afrobank FM, in this case “Tomorrow,” by Ntombi Ndaba, a real South African singer from the late 1980s. GTA often does this, mixing mocking or fictional media with licensed ones in a way that makes you doubt whether you know which element is real and which is invented. That feeling accompanies every moment of life today, because the internet is full of lies that might also be true. Idle Jason nodded his fictional head along to the real Ntombi Ndaba in his fictional Leonida tank top, as if to agree with me.

 S ome of my colleagues in writing and academia—the ones who hate artificial intelligence—have taken to the idea that “writing is thinking.” They use this shorthand as a self-evident takedown of AI. If people had to write (well, presumably?) to think, then nobody would ever think—especially academics. I have to walk to think, so I put down the PlayStation controller to take a walk to try to figure out what I think about Grand Theft Auto VI .

 After you have played a video game, the real world feels more akin to the apparatus you control in a video game. My feet no longer felt like my own as they crunched gravel on the street. Construction is everywhere in my neighborhood, the consequence of a tornado that blew through here 18 months ago. I steered my human body around a hole in the pavement and a construction dumpster at the gutter. A worker was standing between the sidewalk and an approaching pickup truck, and I had to veer uncomfortably close to him to get by.

 As I did, I inhaled the strong smell of his cologne, which vanished as quickly as it appeared. You cannot smell in Grand Theft Auto , a game for the eyes and ears and thumbs. This somehow made smelling seem unimportant, rather than making the game feel insufficiently realistic. The construction worker’s cologne came across as improbable and fake.

 A wardrobe in the corner allows me to change Jason out of his tank top and into other garments—a military outfit, workout wear, pajamas. I switch to swimwear, and the game previews Jason in red trunks and no shirt.

 I find myself studying his body in distressing detail. I’ve been working out seriously for the past two years or so and become occasionally concerned about the tone of my abs, a vanity I find embarrassing to admit. Along the way, I’ve worried that the AI depictions of the human body on YouTube fitness-video previews are giving me body dysmorphia. Jason’s abs look as toned (or less?) than mine, which I had checked in the mirror this morning. This fact makes me feel somehow affirmed—that I am in as good of shape as an animated video-game antihero.

 A triangle appears in Jason’s bathroom, indicating that I can shower. Doing so cuts to a shot of Jason from behind, his naked ass visible under the flowing water. Nudity feels like an attempt to make a video game serious in the way that it once did for cable-television shows. The whole idea has been prudishly outmoded on TV; there, visible vomiting indicates seriousness rather than butts or boobs.

 [ Ian Bogost: Zelda’s midlife crisis ] 

 I can make Jason shower, after a fashion. You pull a trigger on the controller to scrub and, while doing so, use the left joystick to move his hands. Driving is like this too—akin to piloting a vehicle, if a vehicle were a marionette instead of a machine. Getting clean increases Jason’s focus. When he emerges from the shower (hold a button to dress), Jason is still carrying the coffee mug.

 Years ago, I took my son to the empty parking lot of a local shopping mall to teach him to drive. He struggled with hand-over-hand steering, because video games had given him a false idea about the process of driving a vehicle. Driving in video games has always overstated the sensitivity of steering. (A few years later, my daughter, who had played only Nintendo’s Animal Crossing , had no such trouble.)

 Jason drives a beat-up Chevy El Camino, which is fictionalized as the Cheval Picador in the series. Although GTA has always encouraged reckless driving, I had heard that you have to be more careful in this game, because you need to repair your car if it gets damaged, and that requires money, which demands in-game work. But the game frustrated my attempts to drive properly, as if the ghosts of its prior iterations were haunting the new doctrine of vehicular realism. Backing up has always been a freak show in GTA , and I immediately blew out a taillight.

 When I regained composure, I found myself commuting, for real. I kept two car lengths back in traffic. I stopped at stop signs in the middle of nowhere. I took turns wide and felt guilty when my perception of the road, unaided by the embodiment that would make real driving easy, caused me to mistake an oncoming lane for my own. When I arrived at Jason’s house, where the map had guided me, I accidentally pulled into a neighboring property. It was night and hard to see. I felt guilty, the way you do when your Uber from the airport pulls into a neighbor’s driveway instead of your own.

 Y ears ago, a less adept game with similarly adult ambitions, called Heavy Rain , allowed the player to intervene in narrative cutscenes via a technique known as quick-time events. Early on, the player loses track of a child named Jason in a mall. This failure turns tragic and motivates the rest of the story (which is, alas, stupid). The game instructs the player, who is frantically searching for Jason, to press “X” to call out for him. This mortifying depiction of human terror became a meme, at a time when memes were still new: “Press X to Jason.”

 Surely, it is no accident that one of the main characters in GTA VI is also named Jason. Pressing “X” to Jason has finally grown up, not because the act is more serious but because the world has acclimated to it. Press “X” to dinner in DoorDash. Press “X” to time off in Workday. Press “X” to health care in MyChart.

 Someone told me that they heard Grand Theft Auto VI begins with a lot of cutscenes. That is not quite right. It begins with paperwork. Accept the license agreement. Affirm the privacy policy. Choose your heads-up-display design. Calibrate the brightness and color gamut of your monitor. Enable subtitles or select on-screen-text size. Games such as this one have longed to meet or replace Hollywood films for decades. In some ways, they have.

 In others, the reverse has taken place. Watching television or cinema—which one does at home now, principally—involves operating software services as much as consuming media: scrolling menus, running updates, scanning QR codes to log in.

 T he French theorist Jean Baudrillard knew about the future—our present—decades before time revealed it to you and me. Everything would become simulation, a barrage of representation replacing lived reality. These were ideas, complex and hard-to-read ones. Baudrillard also anticipated the form of the internet age, with its short bursts of disconnected meaning. He wrote many books entirely from aphorisms, including one about America (called America ) and a series on anything he could think of (called Cool Memories ). Just as the photographer Stephen Shore accidentally invented Instagram in the 1970s, so Baudrillard accidentally invented Twitter in the 1980s.

 Two weeks ago, culling some of the many books in my office, I donated a couple of boxes of ’80s and ’90s theory that felt irrelevant today. But I kept America and Cool Memories . I have always yearned to write like that, like Baudrillard, in aphorism rather than argument. GTA VI finally justified it, by turning life (or its simulation) into a series of disconnected rituals.

 I have to make a disclosure. Take-Two Interactive, the company that owns Rockstar Games, the creator of GTA VI , has paid me a lot of money over the years for legal consulting related to intellectual-property litigation.

 One of those cases involved the parent company’s sports games, such as the NBA 2K series, made by the Take-Two subsidiary 2K Games. A tattoo artist had sued Take-Two for reproducing the tattoos he had inked on LeBron James’s actual body, which he claimed the game developer needed permission to reproduce in virtual form, despite the fact that 2K Games had secured the rights to James’s (and every other NBA player’s) likeness via an agreement with the NBA. The realism of the games was central to the dispute.

 [ Listen: Will the new Grand Theft Auto be a weapon in the culture wars? ] 

 During the trial’s testimony, the opposing counsel showed me a version of NBA 2K that his litigation team had configured to play with two teams composed entirely of LeBron Jameses. “Is this realistic?” the attorney challenged. “Yes,” I responded. What he showed amounted to a realistic depiction of what reality would look like were you to stage a professional basketball game composed entirely of James clones.

 Take-Two won the case .

 O ut on Jason’s deck, ring marks on the wooden railing caps look like they have been painted on rather than worn in as moisture. When I look across the swampy bog surrounding the house, everything is too bright. The shadows don’t look dark enough, and the highlights appear too washed out. It looks like a high-dynamic-range computer rendering.

 Or it did, before the software in smartphones, which are the devices people now use to take photographs, started performing intensive processing, including high dynamic range. That’s why what you see in the world tends to look deep-fried in your pictures. That style is now so commonplace that it has become what a photograph looks like—what the world looks like, once it is shared as photographs on social media.

 There, looking across the HDR water of the Leonida Keys, I held a button on the controller to put down the mug Jason was still holding. He set it on the wood railing cap overlooking the swamp. There, the software gave it a label, Mug , and a triangle icon indicating that I could pick it up again.
